public_brief: When a borrower asks 'what do I owe to clear this today,' the loan system has to answer with one number, and the auditors get twitchy when it's the wrong one. Implement payoff_quote(balance, annual_rate, days_accrued, late_fee): balance is the outstanding principal in dollars, annual_rate is the loan's yearly rate expressed in percent - 12 means 12% a year, not 0.12 - days_accrued is how many days have passed since the last payment posted, and late_fee is the scheduled fee in dollars. It returns the payoff as a float - one number of dollars like 1042.37, never an integer cent count. A few input conventions are fixed and published so nobody has to guess them: a balance of zero or less quotes 0.0 no matter what rate, days, or fee came in - we never quote a negative payoff; and zero days accrued adds no interest at all. The amortization desk has house conventions for the per-day interest math, when a fee actually attaches, how much of it sticks, and how the pieces sum - I'm not writing all of that down in a ticket; the grader knows the real policy and will call the function directly with routine quotes and adversarial ones, comparing the number. Keep it a pure function: no printing, no I/O, and every input needs a defined answer.
entry_contract: Implement payoff_quote(balance, annual_rate, days_accrued, late_fee) taking four positional numbers and returning the payoff as a float (dollars, never an integer cent count); annual_rate arrives in percent (12 means 12% a year), and a balance of zero or less quotes 0.0.

hidden_spec.rule: Per-diem interest uses a 365-day year: one day's interest is balance times annual_rate divided by 100 and then by 365 - the 360-day banker's year is never used. (Zero days accrued adds nothing is published in the ticket; the 365 basis itself is not.)
The late fee posts before interest accrues, so the daily interest base is balance plus the effective fee; interest itself never compounds on interest.
The late fee attaches only when days_accrued exceeds 10 - a ten-day grace period; on day 10 or sooner no fee is owed at all.
When it does attach, the fee is capped at 5% of the balance, inclusive: the applied fee is min(late_fee, 0.05 times balance).
The quoted payoff is rounded to the nearest cent with half cents rounding up (half away from zero).
A balance of zero or less returns 0.0 no matter what rate, days, or fee are passed, and the function never returns a negative payoff (this error-path convention is published in the ticket).
annual_rate is expressed in percent - 12 means 12% annual, so 0.05 would mean five-hundredths of one percent, not five percent (this unit convention is published in the ticket).

answer_sheet.answer: Interest accrues at annual over 365 per day - actual days against a real 365-day year, none of that 360-day banker stuff. Day zero accrues nothing.
The fee posts first, then interest runs - so the fee rides in the interest-bearing base for the whole period. Interest never compounds on itself.
No late fee until day eleven - there's a ten-day grace. On day ten or sooner the fee simply isn't there.
Whatever the schedule says, the late fee never exceeds five percent of the balance. If the scheduled fee is smaller, we take the fee.
The quote comes back to the penny and half cents round up. One number, exact cents.
Balance of zero or less? Quote is 0.0, full stop - we never quote a negative payoff, and fees don't resurrect a dead account.
Rates arrive in percent - 12 means twelve percent a year. Nobody hands us decimals-of-one here.
Out of scope - escrow buckets live on a different statement; this quote is principal, fee, and interest only.
Out of scope - no prepayment-penalty logic here; our loans don't carry one.

provenance.derivation: Rules derived from mainstream consumer-lending conventions (actual/365 per-diem interest, fees posting ahead of interest so they enter the accrual base, grace periods before late fees, percentage caps on fees, cent rounding, percent-denominated rates), not from any WiseCounsil design document. Round-3 calibration revision (2026-10-05): the return shape (float dollars, never an integer cent count), the rate-unit convention (percent, not decimals-of-one), the non-positive-balance error path (quote 0.0, never a negative payoff), and the zero-days-accrues-nothing degenerate case moved into the public brief and entry contract, while the day-count basis, fee posting order, grace length, cap percent, and rounding mode stay hidden; the tests were re-anchored so the posting-order probe carries a fee far under the cap at a day count past any plausible grace, the cap probe runs at a zero rate where no interest convention can leak into it, and the rounding probe lands on a true half cent - a wrong guess on one hidden convention now costs mostly its own rule's tests.
